passage:
Paragraph A
A volcano that is about to erupt does not announce the fact. What it does instead is behave slightly differently from the way it behaved last month, and the whole discipline of eruption forecasting rests on being able to notice that difference. This turns out to be a harder requirement than it sounds, because it means the interesting measurements are not the ones taken during a crisis but the ones taken during years in which nothing at all appears to be happening.

Paragraph B
Forecasting is done on two quite different timescales. Longer-term forecasts, usually called hazard assessments, are built from an individual volcano's geological past. By dating and measuring the deposits of well-characterised earlier eruptions, scientists establish how often that volcano erupts, how large those eruptions tend to be, and what style they take — whether it produces slow lava flows, explosive ash columns, or the fast avalanches of hot gas and rock that are the most lethal of all. This tells a planning authority what kind of event to prepare for, but nothing whatever about when.

Paragraph C
Short-term forecasting is the other business, and it depends on real-time monitoring during a period of unrest. The key to success is recognising when a volcano is moving away from its background level of activity. That phrase carries the whole difficulty: a background level is not something that can be established after the unrest begins. It has to be measured during quiescence, over long unglamorous stretches when the instruments record nothing remarkable, so that when a change does occur there is something to compare it against.

Paragraph D
The most consistent sign of volcanic unrest is earthquake activity. Magma forcing its way upward fractures rock, and the resulting small earthquakes cluster beneath the volcano at depths that shallow as the magma rises. Seismologists watch not only for the number of events but for their character: a swarm of ordinary brittle-failure earthquakes means one thing, while a continuous low-frequency tremor, produced by fluid moving through cracks, means something rather different and usually more urgent.

Paragraph E
The second family of signals concerns the shape of the mountain. Magma accumulating in a reservoir takes up room, and the ground above it swells — sometimes by a few millimetres, occasionally by a great deal more. Ground deformation is measured by tiltmeters, by satellite positioning receivers fixed to the flanks, and by radar images taken from orbit and compared against earlier ones. The bulge that grew on the north flank of Mount St Helens in 1980, advancing outward by metres a day, remains the most spectacular instance of a volcano visibly changing shape before an eruption.

Paragraph F
The third family is chemical. Magma at depth holds dissolved gases, and as it rises and the pressure falls those gases come out of solution and escape through the ground and the summit vents. A rising output of sulphur dioxide is a particularly useful indicator of magma moving underground, and it is measured by pointing an ultraviolet spectrometer at the plume and calculating how much of the sunlight passing through it has been absorbed. Changes in the proportions of the gases can matter as much as the total quantity.

Paragraph G
No single one of these signals is sufficient. Volcanoes produce swarms of earthquakes that lead nowhere, ground swells that subside again, and gas surges that mean only that a crack has opened. Confidence comes from the signals agreeing with one another, and from their agreeing with what the volcano's own geological record says it is capable of. This is why a comprehensively instrumented volcano can be forecast usefully while a poorly instrumented one of the same type cannot, and why the majority of the world's dangerous volcanoes, which have almost no instruments at all, remain effectively unwatched.

Paragraph H
What, then, can be promised? Most scientists think the build-up preceding a catastrophic eruption would be detectable for weeks, and perhaps for months or years. At Mount St Helens, once the crisis was under way, a series of eruptions was forecast correctly as much as three weeks ahead. But these are statements about detection, not about precision. Forecasting a volcano is closer to forecasting an illness than to forecasting an eclipse: the signs can be read with growing confidence as the event approaches, and the date is not among the things they give you.

(Glossary: quiescence: a period of inactivity; tiltmeter: an instrument that measures very small changes in the slope of the ground; tremor: continuous shaking, as opposed to separate earthquakes; plume: the column of gas and ash rising from a vent.)
